Uncoordinated teams working on closely related applications may race ahead but produce parts that do not fit, ending up spending more on translation layers and retrofitting, duplicated effort, and a lost common language than continuous integration would have cost.

When one subsystem feeds another with one-way dependency, establish a Customer/Supplier relationship in which the downstream team plays the customer role in the upstream team's planning, and downstream requirements are negotiated and budgeted so the commitment and schedule are understood.
condition: when there is a one-directional upstream/downstream dependency

statement: Jointly develop automated acceptance tests that validate the interface the downstream expects and add them to the upstream team's continuous-integration suite, so the upstream can change code without fear of breaking downstream and the downstream need not constantly monitor the upstream.
Treat any change to the shared customer/supplier acceptance tests as implying a change to the interface, requiring communication with the other team.

The two crucial elements of a customer/supplier relationship are that the customer's needs are paramount (balanced among multiple customers, not a poor-cousin begging relationship) and that an automated test suite lets each team work without constantly monitoring the other.

A customer/supplier relationship is more likely to succeed when the two teams work under the same management and thus share goals, or when they are separate companies that genuinely occupy those commercial roles.

When an upstream team has no motivation to serve the downstream, do not naively apply a cooperative pattern; the downstream's realistic options are to go separate ways, build an anticorruption layer, or conform to the upstream model.
condition: when upstream and downstream are not effectively directed from the same source

statement: Do not make downstream plans based on an upstream team's altruistic promises, because belief in good intentions that go unfulfilled leads to planning around features that never arrive and delays the project.

When the quality is acceptable and you have a large interface to an off-the-shelf or upstream component, become a Conformist by slavishly adhering to its model to eliminate translation complexity and share a ubiquitous language, accepting the cost of dependency and being limited to that model plus additive enhancements.
condition: when the upstream design is good enough and the interface is large
exception: when the interface is small, translation is viable instead of conforming

statement: When the upstream dependency is indispensable but its design is too difficult to work with, the downstream team must develop its own model and take full responsibility for an anticorruption-layer translation rather than conforming.
condition: when upstream design lacks encapsulation or uses an unusable paradigm but cannot be abandoned

statement: Create an Anticorruption Layer: an isolating layer that provides clients functionality in terms of their own domain model, talking to the other system through its existing interface and translating in both directions, so the new model is not corrupted by undigested foreign elements.
condition: when a new system must integrate heavily with a legacy or external system based on a different model

statement: An anticorruption layer is a mechanism that translates conceptual objects and actions between two models and protocols, not merely a mechanism for sending messages or transporting data between systems.

Do not assume that primitive data transported between systems has the same meaning on both sides, because important differences arise from how the data are associated in each system, and a low-level interface forfeits the other model's power to explain and constrain the data.

Present the anticorruption layer's public interface as a set of Services (occasionally an Entity), each with a coherent responsibility in terms of your model, reabstracting the external system's behavior rather than representing it as a single component.

Organize an anticorruption layer as a combination of facades, adapters, and translators plus the needed communication mechanisms, separating the adapter's job of making a request from the translator's distinct task of converting conceptual objects or data.

Write a facade for the other system strictly in accordance with that system's own model, keeping it in the other system's bounded context, because building it to your model diffuses translation responsibility or creates yet a third model belonging to neither context.
exception: the facade may be omitted when the other subsystem is simple or has a clean interface

statement: Keep a translator lightweight and stateless, instantiated when needed and belonging with the adapters it serves, so translation logic stays easy to understand.

Integration is always expensive, ranging from continuous integration inside one context down to the defensive anticorruption layer, so confirm the integration is really needed and balance the benefits of isolation against its costs.

Use an anticorruption layer to support a gradual transition from a legacy system, letting a minimal new application delegate to the legacy through translation and then take over functions or add value release by release while continually operating the combined system.

Ruthlessly scope requirements and declare a bounded context to have no connection to others (Separate Ways) when two sets of functionality have no indispensable relationship, because features being related in a use case does not mean they must be integrated.
condition: when two functional parts do not call each other, share interacting objects, or share operating data

statement: Integration forces compromises, because a simple specialized model that satisfies a particular need must give way to a more abstract model that handles all situations.

Cutting loose low-value integrations can deliver several valuable capabilities almost overnight and distill the remaining requirements, but going Separate Ways forecloses options because models developed in complete isolation are hard to merge later.

When a subsystem is in high demand for integration by many others, define an Open Host Service: a protocol exposing the subsystem as a cohesive set of services, opened for all integrators and enhanced for new needs, rather than maintaining a custom translator for each consumer.
condition: when a subsystem must be integrated with many others and its resources form a cohesive set of services

statement: Keep an open host's shared protocol simple and coherent by handling a single team's idiosyncratic needs with a one-off translator rather than bloating the shared protocol.
Use a well-documented shared Published Language as the common interchange medium between models, translating into and out of it, rather than forcing parties to adopt each other's domain models.

Do not use one application's internal domain model as the data-interchange language, because it then becomes frozen and cannot evolve freely to meet new development needs while serving the ongoing communication role.

When one of the two collaborating models is already a published, well-specified language (such as a documented database interface or an industry XML standard), reuse it as the interchange language rather than introducing a third one.
condition: when a suitable published language already exists

statement: If no integration is required, it does not matter that two models are not unified; if integration is required, much value comes simply from recognizing where the models disagree so the teams do not unknowingly talk at cross-purposes.

Unifying multiple models almost always means creating a new model rather than having one party adopt another's, and successful unification hinges on minimalism, dropping the incidental and incorrect aspects of each original model.

A unified model does not have to reach full maturity in its first version; a crude part-whole integration can serve immediate needs and be deepened later as new requirements and improved understanding drive refinement.

Base decisions about whether to expand or partition bounded contexts on the cost-benefit trade-off between the value of independent team action and the value of rich direct integration, while recognizing that political and reporting structures often determine the outcome in practice.

Larger bounded contexts are favored by smoother flow between user tasks, the ease of understanding one model over two plus mappings, the difficulty of translation, and shared-language team communication.

Smaller bounded contexts are favored by reduced communication overhead, easier continuous integration with smaller teams and code bases, lower demand for scarce abstract-modeling skills, and the ability to cater to specialized user jargon and dialects.

Deep integration of functionality between different bounded contexts is impractical; integration is limited to those parts of one model that can be rigorously stated in terms of the other, which makes sense only for a small interface.

Do not take for granted that an external or legacy system is a single coherent bounded context, since most external systems only weakly meet the definition and often contain semantic contradictions between their parts; check whether their development is well integrated.

Choose Conformist only for a peripheral extension to a system that will remain dominant and do it wholeheartedly (extension only, no modification of the existing model); when the new system is more than an extension, has a small interface, or the other system is badly designed, build your own context with a translation or anticorruption layer.
Maintain roughly one team per bounded context: a single team can maintain multiple contexts, but it is hard for multiple teams to work on one context together.

Catering to specialized user jargon with distinct models carries real costs (reduced shared language, integration overhead, duplicated effort) and the risk of becoming an excuse for any parochial model, so weigh the genuine value of a user group's jargon against rationalized variations that have no value.

You cannot plan on a deep model that unifies distinct languages, because deep models emerge late after much knowledge crunching if at all; accept the opportunity when it arises, change strategy, and refactor.

When improving a project already under way, first define bounded contexts according to the true current practice of the teams (not an ideal organization), tighten continuous integration and translation within that reality, name the contexts in the ubiquitous language, and only then change boundaries in small pragmatic pieces.

Breaking up bounded contexts is relatively easy, but merging them or changing their relationships is challenging and must be done as a planned series of manageable steps rather than a single refactoring.

When merging two contexts toward a shared kernel, first ensure each context is internally unified, set up the sharing process and test suite before any shared code, and start with a small, generic, non-core subdomain (ideally one already being translated) to establish the process.

Defer merging two models that have conformed to the specialized jargon of different user communities until a breakthrough to a deep model provides a language capable of superseding both, because a forced merger may sacrifice the specialized power both models provided.
condition: when the two models serve distinct specialized user needs

statement: Phase out a legacy system incrementally in small iteration-sized units behind an anticorruption layer, deciding a testing strategy up front, since a better-designed legacy system is easier to dismantle a little at a time than a badly designed one.

Let the feasibility of a deployment plan feed back into where context boundaries are drawn, since a translation-layer boundary lets one context be updated independently while a shared kernel imposes a much greater coordination burden on both development and deployment.
Keep a published interchange language stable and do not equate it with the host's model, so the host model can still be refactored freely while the shared language supports ongoing communication.

Do not break a large bounded context into smaller pieces merely because its model seems too complex to comprehend, since that fragmentation loses opportunities; first try distillation and large-scale structure to make the big model tractable.
condition: when the context addresses compelling integration needs and is feasible apart from model complexity
exception: if the large context is not organizationally keepable and is in reality fragmenting, redraw boundaries you can keep

statement: Strategically distill the domain model to help everyone grasp the overall design, identify a core model of manageable size for the ubiquitous language, guide refactoring, focus work on the highest-value areas, and guide outsourcing, off-the-shelf, and assignment decisions.
Identify the Core Domain as the parts of the model that are distinctive and central to the application's purpose, and recognize it as where the most value should be added in the system.

Counteract the tendency of the most skilled developers to gravitate toward technical infrastructure and generic problems, because leaving the specialized core to less-skilled developers produces an application that never does compelling things for users no matter how good the infrastructure is.

Boil the model down to find the core domain, make it easy to distinguish from the supporting model and code, bring its most valuable and specialized concepts into sharp relief, and keep the core small.

Apply top talent to the core domain and recruit accordingly, spend the effort there to find a deep model and supple design, and justify investment in any other part by how it supports the distilled core.

Keep everything outside the core domain as generic as practical, reserve any secrecy for competitive advantage to the core, and when time forces a choice between two refactorings choose the one that most affects the core domain first.

The core domain depends on point of view (one application's core is another's generic component) and should be identified through iterations, since objects that seem central at first may turn out to play supporting roles.

Break the vicious cycle that keeps domain-ignorant top developers on supporting components by pairing strong developers with a long-term commitment to becoming repositories of domain knowledge with one or more domain experts who know the business deeply.

Do not hire short-term outside expertise to build the core domain, because a temporary member is a leak in the accumulating domain knowledge; an expert in a teaching or mentoring role is valuable instead.
exception: an expert in a teaching or mentoring role can be very valuable

statement: The core domain usually cannot be purchased, because the greatest value of custom software comes from total control of the core; back off any framework that constrains the core more than providing reusable generic abstractions.

Apply distillation techniques in escalating order of commitment, from a cheap domain vision statement and highlighted core (little design change) through separating generic subdomains and cohesive mechanisms to a segregated core and finally an abstract core (extensive reorganization).

Identify cohesive subdomains that are not the motivation for your project, factor their generic models into separate modules leaving no trace of your specialties, give their continued development lower priority than the core, and avoid assigning core developers to them.

Prefer a published or formalized model for a generic subdomain when the field already has a robust, widely understood one (such as accounting or physics), implementing only a self-consistent simplified subset rather than reinventing the wheel.
condition: when a well-documented or formalized model is available

statement: Prefer generic subdomains as the place to apply outside or outsourced design expertise, because they do not require deep knowledge of the specialized core, involve little proprietary information, and lessen the training burden for those not committed to deep domain knowledge.
Always cleanly segregate a generic supporting model (such as time zones) from the core domain, because mixing them in makes the core harder to understand and the generic module harder to maintain.

Do not design a generic subdomain for code reusability; model and implement only the part you need now, but be strict about keeping within the generic concept, because introducing industry-specific elements impedes future growth and those elements belong in the core or their own specialized subdomain.

Base the first-cut end-to-end system on some part of the core domain, however simple, rather than an easier supporting generic subdomain, because the core domain is the high-risk part that is often unexpectedly difficult and without which the project cannot succeed.
exception: unless the team has proven skills and the domain is very familiar

statement: Domain-modeling risk is easily underestimated, taking the form of unforeseen complexity, inadequate access to business experts, or gaps in the developers' key skills, and an end-to-end system mitigates risk only insofar as it is an embryonic version of the challenging parts.

Write a short Domain Vision Statement (about one page) describing the core domain and its value proposition, ignoring aspects that do not distinguish this model from others, showing how it balances diverse interests, and revise it as insight grows.

A vision statement alone leaves the specific core elements to individual interpretation, so make the core domain easy to see, because the mental labor of constantly filtering the model to identify key parts absorbs concentration better spent on design.

Highlight the core with a minimalist distillation document (three to seven sparse pages) that describes the core domain and the primary interactions among its elements, written to be understood by nontechnical team members and kept free of mundane detail so it ages slowly.

Alternatively, flag the core elements directly within the primary model repository (highlighter, UML stereotype, code comments) so a developer can effortlessly tell what is in or out of the core, with low effort and low maintenance.

Use the distillation document as a process tool: a change that forces the distillation document to change signals a core-domain change requiring team consultation and notification, while changes outside the core can be made with full developer autonomy.

Rather than refactoring an authoritative but bloated purchased model wholesale, navigate it to identify and flag the handful of sections expressing the essential differentiating concepts, giving the team a shared view of the core to focus on.

When computations grow complex enough to bloat the design and swamp the conceptual 'what' with mechanistic 'how', first seek a model that makes the computation simple, then partition any conceptually coherent part of the mechanism into a separate lightweight framework.

Partition a Cohesive Mechanism into a separate framework exposed through an intention-revealing interface so the domain elements focus on expressing the problem (the what) and delegate the intricacies of the solution (the how) to the framework, leaving a smaller, more declarative core.

Watch for formalisms or well-documented categories of algorithms (such as graph theory) when extracting a cohesive mechanism, because basing it on a studied, documented formalism lets you implement with confidence and little trial and error and lets other developers look it up.

Distinguish a Generic Subdomain from a Cohesive Mechanism by responsibility: a generic subdomain is an expressive model that represents some aspect of the domain (a model proposes), while a cohesive mechanism does not represent the domain but solves a computational problem the models pose (a mechanism disposes).

Almost always remove mechanisms from the core domain, the one exception being a mechanism that is itself proprietary and a key part of the software's value, such as a distinctive specialized algorithm.
exception: a proprietary mechanism that is a key part of the software's value belongs in the core

statement: Pragmatic refactoring may reabsorb a separated mechanism when the extra object count and packaging overhead are not warranted, while retaining the declarative public interface and keeping the mechanism encapsulated, yielding a deeper model that more clearly differentiates facts, goals, and mechanisms.

An exceptional payoff comes when part of the core domain breaks through to a deep model with a supple design that functions as a language whose elements combine to express the most important application scenarios, letting client code take on a distilled declarative style.

Create a Segregated Core by refactoring to separate the core concepts from supporting players, strengthening the core's cohesion and reducing its coupling, and moving generic or supporting elements into other packages even when this splits a previously cohesive module.

Segregating the core is a lot of work and can make some non-core relationships more obscure, so do it when a large bounded context critical to the system has its essential model obscured by supporting capability, accepting the cost because the enterprise-specific aspects add the most value.
condition: when a large critical context's essential model is obscured by supporting capability

statement: Move the entire team to a segregated core together through a joint decision process agile enough for repeated course corrections, constraining everyone to the same definition of the core while letting that definition evolve and forbidding individuals from acting on new core insights unilaterally.

Identify the core by what the domain vision statement says the system is for and who uses it, relegating other concerns (such as billing for an operations application) to supporting roles rather than assuming the obvious bottom-line concern is the core.
Segregating the core surfaces new insights, such as a constraint that proves fundamental, and motivates refactoring associations so the most important scenarios are as simple and direct as possible.
Recognizing useful, meaningful modules is itself a modeling activity in which developers and domain experts collaborate in strategic distillation as part of knowledge crunching.

When many interactions span separately packaged subdomains, factor the most fundamental domain concepts into abstract classes or interfaces (an Abstract Core) placed in their own module that expresses most of the cross-component interaction, leaving specialized implementations in subdomain modules that reference the abstract core but not each other.
condition: only when the polymorphic interfaces correspond to fundamental domain concepts

statement: Factoring out an abstract core is not mechanical: automatically moving every frequently cross-referenced class into a module yields a meaningless mess, so it requires deep understanding of the key concepts and is an act of refactoring to deeper insight.

Distillation also means continuously refactoring the subdomains, especially the core, toward a deep model and supple design that expresses the domain simply, because a deep-model breakthrough in the core can change the trajectory of an entire project.

Choose refactoring targets deliberately rather than refactoring everywhere or only where it hurts: in pain-driven refactoring fix the root first if it involves the core or the core's relationship to a supporting element, and when free to refactor focus on better factoring the core, improving core segregation, and purifying supporting subdomains to be generic.

The pain-driven approach of refactoring only what hurts tends to pick around the edges, treating symptoms and ignoring root causes, leaving the worst tangles until the code becomes harder and harder to refactor.

Introduce a Large-Scale Structure: a set of high-level concepts or rules that establishes a design pattern for the entire system and lets each part's role in the whole be understood without detailed knowledge of every other part.

A large-scale structure usually spans more than one bounded context, complementing distillation by holding together all the teams and subsystems; most such structures shape and explain the model without appearing in it and need not be represented in UML.

Do not impose a large-scale structure up front; let the conceptual structure evolve with the application, possibly changing to a completely different type, and do not overconstrain the detailed design decisions that require detailed knowledge.

Architectures that freeze many up-front design decisions become a straitjacket as requirements change and understanding deepens, so the problem is not the existence of guiding rules but their rigidity and source; rules that genuinely fit the circumstances push development in a helpful direction.

Choosing a large-scale structure favors manageability of the whole over optimal structuring of individual parts, so mitigate the compromise by selecting the structure from actual domain experience, avoiding over-constrictive structures, and keeping it applicable across bounded contexts.

Large-scale structure is optional (unlike the context map): impose one only when costs and benefits favor it and a fitting structure is found, since an ill-fitting structure is worse than none; prefer a minimal set over comprehensiveness, and flag any exceptions.
exception: simple systems understood through well-named modules need no large-scale structure

statement: Adopt a System Metaphor only when a concrete analogy emerges that captures team members' imagination and leads thinking in a useful direction; organize the design around it, absorb it into the ubiquitous language, and continually reexamine it for overextension or inaptness, dropping it if it gets in the way.
condition: only when an apt, evocative analogy presents itself

statement: Few projects find a genuinely useful system metaphor, and a persuasive but inexact metaphor risks the design taking on undesirable aspects of the analogy, so do not force a metaphor onto a domain where it is counterproductive.

A mature domain model is not a naive metaphor; the role a system metaphor would play can be fulfilled by the ubiquitous language, and a large-scale structure or metaphor should be added only when one fits well.

Apply responsibility-driven design at large scale by imposing structure on the assignment of responsibilities, since handcrafting each object's responsibilities individually gives a large model no uniformity and no way to handle broad swaths of the domain together.

Define Responsibility Layers by identifying natural strata in the domain (parts that change at different rates and for different reasons), casting them as broad abstract responsibilities that tell the system's high-level story, and refactoring so each object, aggregate, and module fits within one layer.
condition: when the domain has a natural stratification

statement: Use the Relaxed Layered System variant for responsibility layers, allowing a component of one layer to access any lower layer rather than only the layer immediately below it.

Treat the choice of which layer a concept belongs to as a business-modeling decision that captures and communicates domain knowledge, not a technical decision (for example placing Customer in the potential layer because the business cultivates long-term relationships).

A large-scale structure grounded in deep domain understanding will often push the model in directions that clarify its meaning, such as extracting a policy attribute into an explicit policy object so a lower-layer concept stays focused on its fundamental responsibility.

Once a large-scale structure is adopted, make subsequent modeling and design decisions respect it and reject an otherwise appealing design that violates the structure (such as an operational object depending on a decision-support object), because consistent team decisions make the whole design comprehensible and are worth modest detailed trade-offs.
exception: if the structure forces many awkward design choices, evaluate and perhaps modify or discard it

statement: Look for and preserve three characteristics in good responsibility layers: storytelling (they communicate the business's basic realities and priorities), conceptual dependency (upper-layer concepts are meaningful against lower layers while lower-layer concepts stand alone), and conceptual contours (the layer accommodates shearing between elements with different rates or sources of change).

Recurring responsibility layers for enterprise systems include Potential (what resources can do), Operations (what is being done), Decision Support (what action or policy to choose), Policy (the rules and goals), and Commitment (what has been promised), and certain layers recur across families of related domains.
Keep operational objects free to reference or be composed of potential objects, but never let a potential object reference the operations layer, preserving the one-directional conceptual dependency.

An intrinsic advantage of layers is that lower layers can exist without the higher ones, which facilitates phased introductions and building higher-level enhancements on top of older operational systems.

Keep a layering system simple, ideally no more than four or five layers, because too many layers tell the story poorly and reintroduce the very complexity the structure was meant to solve; the large-scale structure must be ferociously distilled.

Do not force a domain into a standard set of layers; if the well-known layers do not capture a domain's salient responsibilities, devise original ones using intuition and let the order evolve from a chosen starting point.

Implement a Policy layer in the same model as the layers it constrains even when using a rules engine, because writing rules against a different model than the objects they apply to either explodes complexity or forces the objects to be dumbed down.

When configurable behavior is needed, neither a fully general model nor a highly customized one serves users well, because customizing per organization is impractical and adding flexibility options to model objects makes them unwieldy as complexity explodes.

When a data field starts to represent an important domain concept that should enforce policy (such as a job title that determines pay and retirement plan), refactor it into an explicit type object whose configuration is restricted to a superuser changing it only when policy changes.

Apply a Knowledge Level to separate the self-defining part of a model into a distinct set of objects that describe and constrain the structure and behavior of the basic model, keeping a concrete operations level and a customizable knowledge level that a user or superuser can adjust.
condition: when roles and relationships among entities must be configured at installation or runtime

statement: Build a domain Knowledge Level out of ordinary domain objects rather than the programming language's reflection tools, focusing on the application domain and deliberately not striving for full generality, because a specialized set of constraints communicates the designer's intent better than a generalized framework.

Use the Knowledge Level sparingly and only where customization is crucial, because its indirection adds obscurity, a complex knowledge level forces configuring users to need programmer-level skills, data-migration problems persist, and it places a heavy burden on the designer to handle any future configuration.

A Knowledge Level differs from Responsibility Layers because dependencies run in both directions between its levels, and it can coexist with most other large-scale structures as an additional dimension of organization.

Organizing a model by an explicit knowledge level can reveal further clarifying insights, such as recognizing that two distinct concepts (for example payroll and employee type) were combined in one object and should be factored apart.

Watch for a statement spoken in the language the team wants rather than the language the model actually supports (a term in conversation that has no element in the model), because it signals an implicit concept lumped into another object that should be made explicit.

Build a Pluggable Component Framework by distilling an abstract core of interfaces and interactions and creating a framework in which diverse implementations of those interfaces can be freely substituted and any application can use the components strictly through the abstract core.
condition: only after several applications have been built in the same mature, deep, distilled domain

statement: A pluggable component framework should not be the first or second large-scale structure applied on a project, because it requires precise interface design and a deep model, limits applications to one approach to the core, and effectively freezes the core's continued refactoring toward deeper insight.

Treat a pattern such as pluggable components as a conceptual organization of responsibilities, and adopt a technical framework only when it solves an essential technical problem such as distribution or sharing a component among applications.

Communicate an exceptional condition from a lower layer up to a higher one through an event mechanism (lower objects emit events, higher policy objects listen), so signaling does not create two-way dependencies from the lower layers to the higher ones.
condition: when a lower layer must notify a higher one in a layered structure

statement: A more restrictive large-scale structure increases uniformity and pushes developers toward good, well-fitting designs, but may remove flexibility developers need and be impractical across heterogeneous contexts, so resist the temptation to over-regiment and ensure each structural rule actually makes development easier.
The most important contribution of a large-scale structure is conceptual coherence and insight into the domain, not regimentation of the implementation.

Find a fitting large-scale structure only through deep domain understanding gained by iterative development, and fearlessly rethink it throughout the project life cycle rather than saddling the project with a structure conceived early when no one understood the domain.

Keep an evolving large-scale structure minimal and lightweight, addressing only the most serious concerns and leaving the rest case-by-case, and consider starting with a loose structure such as a system metaphor or a couple of responsibility layers.

A large-scale structure is held together only by team self-discipline: incorporate its terminology and relationships into the ubiquitous language and have everyone exercise it relentlessly, because such structures are abstract, not enforced by code or tests, and decay without consistent adherence.

A design that has a large-scale structure is usually much easier to transform than one without, even when changing from one kind of structure to another, because repeated sound transformations embed knowledge and make the principal axes of change flexible while simplifying stable aspects.

Apply continuous distillation to ease restructuring: remove mechanisms and generic subdomains from the core so there is less to restructure, and define supporting elements to fit the structure simply (for example a generic subdomain confined to a single layer or owned by one component).

The three principles of strategic design (bounded context, distillation, and large-scale structure) are complementary rather than substitutes, and a large-scale structure may itself be part of the core domain when it distills an insight fundamental to the business problem.

When a legacy system is inconsistent with your desired large-scale structure, do not abandon the structure; instead characterize the legacy by which layers its services fit within (for example via a facade whose each service fits one layer), which concisely describes its scope and role.

Begin strategic design with an assessment of the current situation: draw a context map and check it is consistent, evaluate whether a rich ubiquitous language exists, confirm the core domain and a domain vision statement, and judge whether the technology and the developers' skills, domain knowledge, and interest support a model-driven design.

Do not hand strategy down from an ivory-tower architecture team detached from application development; let order emerge from a self-disciplined application team (optionally with a hands-on informal leader) or use an architecture team that acts as a hands-on peer, and value the developers' actual relationship with the strategy over management-bestowed authority.

Make the strategic-design decision process absorb feedback through a tight loop with the application development teams, because only they have the depth of domain and project knowledge needed, which is why architectures handed down by detached architecture teams are seldom helpful.

Let the strategic plan allow for evolution, because setting the highest-level decisions in stone hobbles the team's ability to respond to change; a harmonizing principle must grow with the project and not take too much power from application developers.

Do not let architecture and infrastructure teams siphon off all the best developers, because building good applications takes design skill, and a strategic design is useless if the application team lacks the sophistication to follow it.

Ensure strong designers are on every application team and that domain knowledge is present on any team attempting strategic design, because strategic design is not a purely technical task and cutting it off from deep domain knowledge cripples it.

Practice minimalism and humility in strategic design: pare organizing principles and core models down to contain nothing that does not significantly improve clarity, because almost every element gets in the way of something and your best idea is likely to obstruct someone.

Make objects specialists with clear narrow responsibilities and minimal interdependence, but let developers be generalists who cross into each other's areas, since separating design experts from domain experts by overspecialization takes the steam out of domain-driven design.

Develop technical frameworks with the same biases of evolution, minimalism, and involvement with the application team, because an architecture that does not follow this path will either stifle application development's creativity or be circumvented and leave no effective architecture at all.

Do not write frameworks for dummies on the assumption some developers are not smart enough to design, because that underestimates application development and erects barriers; encapsulating irrelevant technical detail to place powerful abstractions in capable developers' hands is the opposite and legitimate.

Avoid a totalitarian master plan that preordains the whole system, because such plans are too rigid to adapt and become obsolete; instead provide a set of principles every contributor applies to each act of piecemeal growth so organic order emerges.

Judge a design's success by how the software serves over time rather than by its stasis, because making a depended-on system opaque turns it into untouchable legacy, while a deep model and supple design facilitate the ongoing change that is the nature of software.

Treat the feedback loop from implementation problems back to the model as a natural part of model-driven design; when a team judges itself too far down the road to change the fundamental model and instead patches the code for efficiency, the code's connection to the model is weakened and value is lost.

Hand off a design with a thorough test suite and a distillation document, because these let a new team explore and build on the design and let the ubiquitous language spark across and continue evolving.

Releasing a working internal version too late, especially in a culture that resists iterative development, exposes model and infrastructure problems at a late, risky, and expensive stage and can sever the loop between implementation and domain modeling.

The defining characteristic of domain-driven design is a priority on understanding the target domain and incorporating that understanding into the software, from which cultivating the language, dissatisfaction with the model, treating continuous refinement as opportunity and an ill-fitting model as risk, and taking design skill seriously all flow.

Treat creating good software as a learning and thinking activity that requires imagination and self-discipline: tools that help us think or avoid distraction are good, but efforts to automate what must be the product of thought are naive and counterproductive.

Use named design patterns as terms in the team's language to move beyond 'everything is an object', because standard patterns let teams avoid reinventing known solutions, enable economical discussion of a design, and prevent designs so idiosyncratic they are hard to communicate.

An Entity is an object defined fundamentally not by its attributes but by a thread of continuity and identity, whereas a Value Object describes a characteristic or attribute and carries no concept of identity.

A Service is an operation offered as an interface that stands alone in the model with no encapsulated state, and stateless means a client can use any of its operations without regard to the element's history.
A deep model is an incisive expression of the primary concerns of the domain experts and their most relevant knowledge that sloughs off superficial aspects and naive interpretations of the domain.

A supple design puts the power of a deep model into the client developer's hands for clear, flexible, robust expressions while also making the design itself easy for the implementer to mold and reshape to accommodate new insight.

An assertion states the correct state of a program at some point independent of how it is achieved, an invariant is an assertion that must hold at all times except during specifically transient situations, and a side effect is any observable change of state resulting from an operation.
A conceptual contour is an underlying consistency of the domain itself which, when reflected in a model, helps the design accommodate change more naturally.

Unification is the internal consistency of a model such that each term is unambiguous and no rules contradict, and a bounded context is the delimited applicability of a particular model that tells team members what must be consistent and what can develop independently.

Model-driven design is a design in which some subset of software elements corresponds closely to elements of a model, together with a process of co-developing a model and an implementation that stay aligned with each other.
A Standalone Class can be understood and tested without reference to any others except system primitives and basic libraries, and a Whole Value is an object that models a single, complete concept.
Strategic design comprises modeling and design decisions that apply to large parts of the system, affect the entire project, and therefore must be decided at the team level.
